title: Morrison Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Morrison wells have a 305 ft median depth, 6.0 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $25,800-$42,500.
h1: Morrison, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
For rural property near Morrison, the well record points to a mountain-bedrock drilling job rather than a shallow, predictable water source. Among permitted wells within 5 miles, the median depth is 305 feet, and the middle half runs from 152 to 527 feet. The median reported yield is 6.0 gallons per minute.

That is useful for budgeting, but it is not a guarantee for a particular lot. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, where water can be controlled by local fractures. Check nearby well records, the permit conditions, septic layout, and the proposed building site before buying or drilling.

sections.heading: Morrison’s well depths reflect fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
Morrison wells are commonly drilled into fractured granite, gneiss, or other mountain bedrock. The recorded median depth is 305 feet. Half of the wells with reported depths fall between 152 and 527 feet, while the 90th percentile is 780 feet. The deepest record reaches 4,095 feet.

The depth mix shows why a single shallow estimate is risky: 15% are under 100 feet, 30% are from 100 to 300 feet, 34% are from 300 to 600 feet, and 21% exceed 600 feet. A driller’s bid should state the assumed footage, what happens if the hole must go deeper, and how casing and grout are handled.

sections.heading: What Morrison wells usually produce
sections.html:
Reported well yields near Morrison have a median of 6.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 3.0 and 9.8 gallons per minute. The largest group, 56%, reports between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Another 34% falls between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

Only 3% report less than 1 gallon per minute, but that small share still matters when evaluating a specific property. A low-yield well can work with adequate storage and careful household use, while a strong yield does not remove the need for water-quality testing. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, storage capacity, and permit use limits before assuming the well supports irrigation or additional residences.

sections.heading: Water levels vary across Morrison’s mountain terrain
sections.html:
The current recorded median static water level is 100 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 38 to 189 feet. That is the depth to water when the well is at rest, not the same as the well’s total drilled depth and not a promise that the water level will remain unchanged during pumping.

The decade series is uneven rather than a clean, continuing decline. Median depth to water was 52 feet in the 1960s, 55 feet in the 1970s, 90 feet in the 1980s, and 185 feet in the 2010s, then 100 feet in the 2020s. Because only 126 records report static water level, use the series as context, not a site-specific forecast.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers active around Morrison
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 3,675 permitted wells within the local search area. Of those, 2,369 are recorded as constructed, and the newest permit year is 2025. Permit activity was highest in the 1970s, with 788 permits, followed by 639 in the 1990s and 461 in the 1980s. The records include 130 permits from the 2020s.

The most frequently listed drillers are Aspen Drilling Company Inc (Beery, Leroy J.) with 294 records, James Drilling Company (Keaton, Michael K.) with 286, and Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert) with 191. These records show local experience, but obtain current licensing, insurance, scope, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: Morrison well drilling cost at the median depth
sections.html:
Fractured mountain bedrock makes footage the main cost variable. The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 305-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $19,800 to $30,500.

A finished system is more than the hole. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, the estimated total is about $25,800 to $42,500 at the median depth. A property requiring a deeper hole, difficult access, longer utility runs, more casing, or additional site work can cost more. Get the bid in writing and ask whether it includes permitting, casing, grout, development, pump installation, water testing, and a production test. The middle-half depth range of 152 to 527 feet is the most useful warning against treating the median as a fixed price.

sections.heading: Risks to investigate before buying or building
sections.html:
Water quantity is only one part of the decision. Within about 10 miles of Morrison, the map shows 107 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 109 historic mine features, and 60 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped locations do not prove a problem on a particular parcel, but they justify a site-specific water test and a review of nearby land uses.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, representing 87% of the local mix. Stock use is 4%, irrigation is 1%, and monitoring is 4%. Confirm that the existing permit matches your intended use. Also verify well-to-septic separation, available drainfield area, access for a rig, driveway grade, power routing, and building setbacks. In fractured rock, dry holes and sharply different results between neighboring lots are possible.

sections.heading: Buying a lot near Morrison: a practical water check
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then review wells in Indian Hills, Idledale, Dakota Ridge, Genesee, and Kittredge as nearby comparison points. Neighboring records can show depth, yield, water level, aquifer description, and the history of drilling in the immediate mountain setting. They cannot replace a site investigation, but they can expose an unrealistic seller estimate.

Before closing, make the water contingency specific. Request the DWR permit and construction report, confirm the well’s legal use, test the water for ordinary household concerns plus contaminants suggested by local history, and ask a driller to comment on access and likely depth. If building, coordinate the well, septic system, driveway, electric trench, and house location before excavation begins. A lot with a workable well still needs enough usable ground for the complete site plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Morrison, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Morrison is 305 feet. The middle half ranges from 152 to 527 feet, 21% are deeper than 600 feet, and the 90th percentile is 780 feet. Mountain fractures make individual results unpredictable, so nearby well records are more useful than a countywide average.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Morrison?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot. At the 305-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $19,800-$30,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $25,800-$42,500. Deeper drilling, difficult access, casing, and longer utility runs can increase the total.

faq.q: How much water do Morrison wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 6.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 3.0 and 9.8 gallons per minute. Some wells produce less than 1 gallon per minute; that group represents 3% of records. Ask for the production test and storage details rather than relying on the local median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Morrison?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that water is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, there are 107 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 109 historic mine features, and 60 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well before occupancy, using a laboratory and a panel appropriate to the property’s nearby land-use history.

faq.q: Can I build a home on a Morrison property with a well?
faq.a: A well permit does not by itself confirm that a lot is ready to build. Most local permits are domestic or household use, representing 87% of the mix. Confirm the permit, water supply, septic area, well-to-septic separation, driveway access, utility routing, and building layout. Colorado DWR requirements and any basin water-rights conditions also need review.
